vignette: María, a 37-year-old Latina hotel manager, has been struggling with the aftermath of a sexual assault that occurred at her workplace several months ago. The traumatic event left deep psychological scars, and María's symptoms have progressively worsened over time. The incident itself was sudden and brutal. One evening, while she was closing up the front desk, an intoxicated guest entered the lobby demanding assistance. Despite her initial refusal to help him alone, he managed to overpower her and assault her in one of the conference rooms. The memory is still vivid but fragmented; she knows what happened but cannot find the words to describe it coherently. What frightened María most was the feeling that there was something wrong with her as a person, a belief that reinforced by the idea that this event happened because of who she is. This negative self-appraisal led her to engage in maladaptive strategies such as overworking and rumination about how to get even with the assailant. Her sense of shame and defectiveness drove her to avoid people who looked similar to those involved in the event, further isolating herself from support. Since the assault, María has come to believe that her body keeps reacting as if she is still in danger, even when she is safe. This heightened state of threat monitoring became a constant presence in her daily life. She found solace in overworking to avoid being alone with her thoughts and the memories that surfaced. However, this overwork also exacerbated her inability to find coherent words for what happened, as the stress made it harder to articulate her experience. María’s memory fragmentation is intertwined with these negative appraisals and maladaptive strategies. Her difficulty in forming a clear narrative about the event has reinforced her sense of shame and body distrust. Each time she attempts to recount what happened, she feels intense shame, which further fuels her rumination and overworking as coping mechanisms. Over time, María’s work performance suffered due to her prolonged absences and erratic behavior. Her colleagues noticed changes in her demeanor but were unsure how to approach the situation. The cumulative effect of these maladaptive behaviors has strained her relationships with both co-workers and her partner. She found herself increasingly isolated, which only deepened her negative self-perceptions. María had come to believe that there was no way out of this cycle; she felt trapped by her own thoughts and memories. What finally brought her to seek help was the realization that her life was becoming unmanageable. The constant fear and shame were overwhelming, and she was most afraid of losing control completely. However, she also hoped for a chance to regain some semblance of normalcy and peace. In therapy, María aims to unravel these interwoven threads of negative appraisals, memory fragmentation, and maladaptive strategies. She hopes to find the words to describe her experience and to break free from the cycle that has bound her since the assault.
